question: Your team proposes splitting an online store into Catalog, Inventory and Ordering services that keep reading the same MySQL schema. What have they built?
options: Microservices, because each service runs in its own container and scales on its own
A distributed monolith: coupled through one schema, now with network calls
A modular monolith, because the code is split by capability over one database
A CQRS system, because each service reads the shared tables in its own shape
explanation: Data ownership and independent deployment define microservices. A shared schema couples the services as tightly as before and adds latency and partial failures. A modular monolith is one deployable, which this is not; containers alone define nothing.

question: In a monolith, checkout reserves stock and creates the order in one database transaction. What replaces that transaction once Inventory is a separate service with its own database?
options: A distributed transaction that EF Core opens across both databases automatically
A `TransactionScope` around both HTTP calls, so a failure rolls back each service
A retry policy on the HTTP call, so the reservation eventually succeeds every time
Eventual consistency: an outbox, idempotent consumers and compensating actions
explanation: Across services there is no shared ACID transaction, so consistency is rebuilt with messaging patterns from module 10. A `TransactionScope` covers local resources, not another service's database behind HTTP, and an HTTP call can time out after the remote side already committed, so retries alone can duplicate it.

question: Early in a product, boundaries keep moving and two developers maintain the code. Which choice do Microsoft's guidance and this lesson favor?
options: A monolith, ideally modular, so boundaries can be found and moved cheaply
Microservices from day one, so the team never has to migrate a monolith later
One service per aggregate, since aggregates are already the consistency boundaries
Serverless functions for every endpoint, so nothing runs when there is no traffic
explanation: Microsoft's e-book notes that natural boundaries may not be clear early, and that cloning a whole instance is often enough to scale. Moving a boundary inside a monolith is a refactor; moving it between services is a migration of data and contracts.

question: Ordering calls Inventory with `AddStandardResilienceHandler()` defaults to reserve stock with `POST /reservations`. Why is that dangerous?
options: The standard handler does not support `POST`, so the request fails before it is sent
The circuit breaker opens on the first failed `POST` and blocks all later reservations
Its retries cover every method, so a timed-out `POST` can reserve stock twice
The attempt timeout cancels the call, which also rolls back the server's reservation
explanation: Microsoft's docs warn that the standard handler retries every method and offer `DisableForUnsafeHttpMethods()`. A request that timed out on the client may have succeeded on the server: cancelling the client side rolls nothing back, so an automatic retry can duplicate the side effect.

question: Two of your services call each other on almost every request and you always deploy them together. What does the boundary guidance suggest?
options: Put a message broker between them, so the calls become asynchronous and they stay apart
Split them into smaller services, so each one has fewer reasons to call the other
Share a domain library between them, so both services always agree on the types
Merge them: chatty calls and joint deployment signal a wrong boundary
explanation: Microsoft's boundary checklist says chatty services and services that must deploy together indicate the split is wrong. Splitting further or sharing a domain library increases coupling; a broker changes the transport, not the coupling.

question: Which situation is the strongest reason to extract a module into its own service?
options: Stable boundary and data, a different scaling need, and a team blocked by shared releases
The solution has passed 100,000 lines and a full build and test run takes ten minutes
A new team member prefers small repositories with one service each, to learn faster
The team is moving to Kubernetes and wants each module as a separate deployment there
explanation: Extraction pays when the business and organizational reasons line up and the platform can operate another service (per-service CI/CD and tracing). Code size, preference or a new platform are not criteria; a slow build in a large codebase with clean modules is better fixed inside a modular monolith.
